title: Resource Mobilization Strategies and Frameworks
subtitle: Raise and keep deposits and other funding at a cost the bank can afford, in a market of high inflation, a 16% policy rate and new competitors
summary: From the deposit products and a 30-day branch plan to cost of funds, the loan-to-deposit ratio, funds transfer pricing and a three-year funding strategy, built on Ethiopian rules and one running bank case.
audience: Branch staff, relationship and customer service officers (Foundational modules); branch managers, deposit and product managers, ALM and strategy staff (Intermediate modules) in Ethiopian banks.
objectives: Explain why deposits are the main funding source of Ethiopian banks and how the bank earns a spread
Describe the bank's deposit products, including youth, women, diaspora and interest-free accounts, and match them to customer needs
Use basic techniques to identify, approach and retain depositors within KYC and fair disclosure rules
Analyse a bank's funding mix, cost of funds and concentration, and set mobilization targets consistent with lending plans, the loan-to-deposit ratio and the risk of a targeted reserve requirement
Design and price deposit products using customer data, competitor rates and funds transfer pricing
Evaluate non-deposit funding: interbank, NBE standing facilities, bonds, equity and development finance lines

runningCase.name: Bank A and its Hawassa Tabor branch
runningCase.text: Bank A (fictional) is a mid-sized Ethiopian private bank. Over five years its deposits grew from Birr 40 billion to Birr 66 billion, but cheap savings and current accounts fell from 75% to 57% of the total, the top 20 depositors rose from 18% to 31%, the average cost of deposits rose from 6.1% to 9.2% and the loan-to-deposit ratio reached 78.8%, above the 72.7% private-bank average reported by the NBE in July 2026. In the Foundational modules, the manager of its Hawassa Tabor branch, Meron Alemu, builds a 30-day plan to raise Birr 60 million. In the Intermediate modules, learners diagnose the bank's funding and present a three-year resource mobilization strategy to a mock management committee.

modules.title: Why resources matter and the deposit products
modules.summary: See why deposits fund an Ethiopian bank, how the bank earns its spread under a 16% National Bank Rate, and what each deposit product offers the customer.
objectives: Explain why deposits are the main funding source of Ethiopian banks and how the bank earns a spread
Describe how the National Bank Rate, inflation and free rate setting under NBE/INT/13/2026 shape deposit pricing
Calculate the real return a saver earns when inflation is high
Describe savings, current, fixed time, youth, women, diaspora and interest-free accounts and match them to customer needs

lessons.title: Why deposits are the main source of funds
body: A bank lends money that is mostly not its own. In Ethiopia, customer deposits are by far the largest source of a bank's funds, ahead of shareholders' equity and borrowing from other banks or the NBE. The interbank market is still developing and few banks issue bonds, so the deposit base sets how much a bank can lend.

Every branch officer is therefore part of the bank's funding team. A savings account opened at a market stall in Hawassa or a payroll account opened at a factory in Bahir Dar adds to the pool that finances the bank's loans to farmers, traders and manufacturers.
Resource mobilization is the planned work of attracting and keeping these funds at a cost the bank can afford, while respecting the NBE's liquidity and consumer protection rules.

visual.caption: Bank A (fictional) funding at the end of Year 5: deposits are about 80% of its Birr 82 billion balance sheet.

example.title: Bank A's balance sheet
example.text: Bank A is a mid-sized Ethiopian private bank used throughout this course. At the end of Year 5 it held total assets of Birr 82 billion, funded by Birr 66 billion of customer deposits, Birr 9.5 billion of equity, Birr 4 billion of other liabilities and only Birr 2.5 billion of borrowing. If its deposits stopped growing, its lending would stop growing too.

lessons.tip: When you open an account, you are not only serving a customer: you are adding to the funds that let your branch lend.

lessons.title: How the bank earns a spread
body: The bank pays interest to depositors and earns interest from borrowers. The difference, after keeping part of the money in cash, reserves and liquid assets, is the net interest income that pays salaries, rent, technology and a return to shareholders.

Not every birr deposited can be lent. The bank must hold reserves with the NBE, keep cash in branches and hold liquid assets such as Treasury bills. A deposit is only as profitable as the share of it that the bank can put to work and the rate it pays to keep it.

parts.label: Interest earned on loans and investments
Interest paid to depositors and lenders

visual.caption: Operating costs and provisions come out of net interest income before any profit is left.

worked.title: What Birr 1,000,000 of savings earns the bank in a year (illustrative)

rows.label: Kept in cash, reserves and liquid assets (assume 25%)
Cost of serving the accounts (assume 2% of balance)

worked.note: The 25% liquid share and the 2% service cost are teaching assumptions, not regulatory ratios. The point is that the gap between 17.5% and 8.0% is much less than 9.5 points of profit.

scenario.title: The customer who sees only the gap
scenario.situation: Hiwot Kebede, a shop owner in Adama, earns 8% on her savings and pays 17.5% on her working capital loan from the same bank. She tells the customer service officer, Yonas Girma, that the bank is making 9.5% on her money.
scenario.question: What is the best way for Yonas to explain the spread?
options: Suggest she move her loan to a microfinance institution
Explain that part of every deposit is held as cash, reserves and liquid assets, and that the bank also pays staff, systems and loan losses out of the spread
Agree that the margin is 9.5% and offer her a better savings rate
Tell her that interest rates are set by the NBE so the bank has no choice
scenario.explain: Only part of each deposit can be lent and the spread must also cover costs and losses. Since NBE/INT/13/2026 the bank, not the NBE, sets its own rates, so blaming the NBE is wrong.

lessons.title: The National Bank Rate and deposit pricing
body: Since 2024 the NBE steers the economy through an interest-rate-based framework. Its policy rate, the National Bank Rate, signals the price of short-term money. At its meeting of 13 July 2026 the Monetary Policy Committee raised it by 1 point to 16% and removed the temporary credit growth cap.

When the policy rate rises, the interbank rate and Treasury bill yields tend to follow, and depositors expect more. Banks compete harder for time deposits, and the cost of funds rises. With the credit cap gone, banks that want to lend more must first find the deposits to fund it.

Since 9 January 2026 each bank sets its own deposit and lending rates. There is no longer an NBE minimum savings rate, so the bank's own pricing decisions, approved by its board, decide how competitive it is.

visual.caption: Figures reported in the MPC No. 7 release of 13 July 2026. Update them from the latest release before each course.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. NBE/INT/13/2026, Interest Rates (As Amended), in force 9 January 2026
regulation.text: Each bank freely sets its demand, savings and time deposit rates and its lending rates; there is no longer a minimum savings rate. Rates must be approved in writing by the bank's board on explicit written criteria and reported to the NBE, together with monthly weighted average rates. Rates on NBE lending and standing facilities are set by the NBE, and interbank rates are negotiated between banks. The directive repeals all earlier interest rate directives.

lessons.tip: If a customer quotes the old 7% minimum savings rate, explain that it no longer exists: each bank now sets its own rates.

lessons.title: Inflation and the real return to savers
body: Savers care about what their money will buy. The real return is the interest rate after inflation. With headline inflation at 13.4% in May 2026, a savings account paying 8% loses purchasing power each year, while a one-year time deposit at about 13.5% only just keeps pace.

This is why many Ethiopian households hold land, livestock, gold or building materials instead of bank balances, and why rate-sensitive customers move money to time deposits or to the bank that pays most. Branch staff should be honest about real returns and sell the other benefits of a bank account: safety, access to credit, payments and a record of saving.

worked.title: Real return on a one-year deposit when inflation is 13.4%

rows.label: One-year fixed time deposit rate (Bank A)

worked.note: The quick subtraction overstates the loss slightly; the exact formula divides one plus the rate by one plus inflation.

example.title: Almaz's savings in Bahir Dar
example.text: Almaz Bekele, a teacher in Bahir Dar, kept Birr 50,000 in a savings account at 8% for a year and received Birr 4,000 of interest. Over the same year the basket of goods she buys rose 13.4%, so what cost Birr 50,000 now costs Birr 56,700. Her Birr 54,000 balance buys less than her original deposit did. Her officer suggested moving the part she would not need for a year into a time deposit and keeping a smaller balance in savings for emergencies.

scenario.title: Gold or a time deposit?
scenario.situation: Mulugeta Desta, a retired civil servant in Dessie, holds Birr 400,000 in savings at 8%. He tells the branch officer he will withdraw it all to buy gold because the bank 'eats' his money.
scenario.question: What should the officer do?
options: Show him the real return of each option, offer a time deposit for the part he will not need soon, and respect his decision
Tell him that savings rates will rise soon because of the NBE
Warn him that gold is illegal to hold
Promise him a rate above inflation to keep the money
scenario.explain: Honest advice that compares real returns and offers a better-matched product keeps trust. Promising a rate the bank has not set, or forecasting NBE decisions, would mislead him.

lessons.title: The core deposit products
body: Each deposit product meets a different need. Savings accounts are for households that save and withdraw from time to time. Current (checking) accounts are for businesses and individuals who make payments, usually with cheques, and normally pay no interest. Fixed time deposits lock money for an agreed term at a higher rate; interest is lost or reduced on early withdrawal.

Banks also design accounts for groups: children and youth accounts opened by a guardian and paid to the child at 18, women's savings accounts, save-for-credit accounts, provident fund and pension accounts, and accounts linked to a mobile wallet so the customer can save and pay from a phone.

items.label: Savings
items.text: Interest-bearing, withdraw any time with a passbook or card.

items.label: Current (checking)
items.text: For payments and cheques; usually no interest; TIN and delinquent list check.

items.label: Fixed time
items.text: Agreed term and rate; interest lost or reduced on early withdrawal.

items.label: Children and youth
items.text: Opened by a guardian; paid to the account holder at 18.

items.label: Women's savings
items.text: Designed around women's savings goals and access to credit.

items.label: Wallet-linked
items.text: Moves money between the account and a mobile wallet.

points: A typical Ethiopian bank sets example minimum opening balances such as Birr 25 for savings, Birr 250 for checking and Birr 100,000 for fixed time deposits; check your own bank's tariff.
Fixed time deposits need a written application and a certificate.
A child's account is opened and operated by the guardian until the child turns 18.

scenario.title: Matching a trader's seasonal cash
scenario.situation: Kebede Ayana sells teff and maize in Nekemte. After harvest he holds about Birr 2 million that he will need in four months to buy stock for the next season, and he makes payments to suppliers every week.
scenario.question: Which product mix should the officer propose?
options: A child savings account in his son's name
A three-year fixed time deposit for the highest rate
A current account for weekly payments plus a fixed time deposit for the amount he will not touch for four months
Put the whole Birr 2 million in a current account
scenario.explain: Matching the term to his need earns him more on idle cash while keeping payments easy. A three-year deposit would cost him interest when he breaks it, and a child's account would not belong to him.

lessons.title: Interest-free deposit accounts
body: Interest-free banking serves customers who do not wish to pay or receive interest. Ethiopian banks may offer it through an interest-free window or as a full-fledged interest-free bank. It has grown fast and is an important way to reach customers who stayed away from conventional banks.

The two main deposit forms are wadiah and mudarabah. A wadiah account is safekeeping: the bank holds and guarantees the money and promises no return. A mudarabah account is a profit-sharing investment: the customer provides the funds, the bank invests them in permitted business, and profit is shared by a ratio agreed in advance. Some banks also use qard accounts, where the customer lends the money to the bank interest free.

left.title: Wadiah (safekeeping)
items: Used like a savings or current account

right.title: Mudarabah (profit sharing)
items: Customer funds, bank manages the investment
Profit shared by an agreed ratio
Suits customers saving for a term

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/72/2019, Interest-free banking
regulation.text: Allows banks to provide interest-free banking services through a dedicated window or as a full-fledged interest-free bank. Check the directive's detailed conditions on products, governance and the use of funds with your bank's interest-free banking unit.

example.title: An interest-free window in Jimma
example.text: Fatuma Ahmed runs a spice wholesale shop in Jimma and had never used a bank because of interest. When Bank A opened an interest-free window at its Jimma branch, she opened a wadiah account for her shop's daily takings and a mudarabah account for Birr 300,000 she wanted to grow over a year. Two traders she buys from opened accounts the next month after she told them about it.

lessons.title: Diaspora and foreign currency accounts
body: Ethiopians living abroad and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin send home large remittances and invest in homes and businesses. Banks offer them foreign currency accounts and birr accounts under the NBE foreign exchange directive, so their money can earn, be used for local payments or be kept in foreign currency.

Under the July 2024 market-based exchange regime, remittances that come through banks receive the freely negotiated rate, which removed much of the reason to use informal channels. Diaspora accounts are a source of both birr deposits and the foreign currency the country needs.
The rules on what may be credited to a diaspora foreign currency account matter. Funds must come from abroad in foreign currency; a credit from a local birr source is an error the branch must catch.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024 (in force 29 July 2024), as amended by FXD/04/2026 (in force 12 February 2026)
regulation.text: FXD/01/2024 sets the rules for foreign currency accounts of non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin, within the market-based exchange regime. FXD/04/2026 removed the minimum foreign currency account deposit, so older manual rules such as a minimum opening balance on diaspora accounts no longer apply.

example.title: Dawit's remittance account
example.text: Dawit Haile works in Washington and used to send money to his mother in Hawassa through an informal agent. After the 2024 reform he opened a diaspora foreign currency account and a linked birr account with Bank A online. His monthly transfer now arrives at the bank's rate, his mother withdraws birr with a card, and he keeps savings in dollars for a house he plans to build.

scenario.title: A credit that does not belong
scenario.situation: During a file review at the Hawassa branch, Tigist Worku finds that a diaspora foreign currency account received a transfer from a local supplier's birr account, converted at the counter.
scenario.question: What should she do?
options: Convert the whole balance back to birr
Treat it as an error: reverse or correct the entry under the bank's procedure, record the exception and brief the staff involved
Leave it, since the customer is the same person
Close the account immediately and report the customer to the police
scenario.explain: Diaspora foreign currency accounts are funded from abroad in foreign currency. The fix is to correct the entry and the process, not to punish the customer for a branch error.

takeaways: Deposits are about 80% of a typical Ethiopian bank's funding, so the deposit base limits how much the bank can lend.
The spread pays for liquidity, staff, systems and losses; it is much smaller than the gap between loan and deposit rates.
The National Bank Rate rose to 16% in July 2026 and the credit cap was removed, which raises competition for deposits.
Under NBE/INT/13/2026 there is no minimum deposit rate; each bank's board sets and reports its own rates.
With inflation at 13.4%, savings accounts give a negative real return, so honest advice and product fit matter.
Match the product to the need: savings, current, fixed time, group accounts, interest-free (wadiah, mudarabah) and diaspora accounts.

quiz.q: What is the largest source of funds for most Ethiopian banks?
quiz.explain: Deposits fund about four fifths of a typical Ethiopian bank's balance sheet.

quiz.q: Since 9 January 2026, who sets the savings rate a bank pays?
options: Each bank, with written board approval, reported to the NBE
The NBE, at a minimum of 7%
quiz.explain: NBE/INT/13/2026 lets each bank set its own rates and removed the minimum savings rate.

quiz.q: A saver earns 8% while inflation is 13.4%. What is the approximate real return?
quiz.explain: (1.08 / 1.134) minus 1 is about minus 4.8%.

quiz.q: Which account promises no return but guarantees the principal?
quiz.explain: Wadiah is safekeeping: the bank guarantees the money and promises no return.

quiz.q: What happens to the interest on a fixed time deposit withdrawn early?
options: It is lost or reduced under the deposit terms
It is transferred to the NBE
It is paid in foreign currency
quiz.explain: Early withdrawal breaks the agreed term, so interest is lost or reduced.

quiz.q: What did the MPC decide on 13 July 2026?
options: Raised the National Bank Rate to 16% and removed the credit growth cap
Cut the National Bank Rate to 12%
quiz.explain: MPC No. 7 raised the rate by 1 point to 16% and ended the temporary credit cap.

modules.title: Know your market, win and keep depositors
modules.summary: Map the deposit segments of an Ethiopian town, use proven mobilization techniques, follow KYC and disclosure rules, and build a 30-day plan for a regional branch.
objectives: Identify the main deposit segments in an Ethiopian branch's catchment, including iddir and equb
Choose mobilization techniques and channels that fit each segment
Apply KYC, fair disclosure and fair advertising rules when opening and promoting accounts
Handle inactive and dormant accounts and use them as a source of deposits
Build a 30-day deposit mobilization plan with segments, products, channels and a birr target

lessons.title: Deposit segments in Ethiopia
body: Every branch draws its deposits from a mix of customer groups. Knowing who lives and works in the catchment, how they earn and when they have cash is the first step of any mobilization plan.

Segments differ in size, cost and stability. Salaried staff bring many small, stable balances. Traders bring larger, seasonal balances. Cooperatives and institutions bring big amounts that may leave at once. Diaspora families bring remittances and foreign currency.

items.label: Urban salaried
items.text: Civil servants, teachers, factory workers: payroll and savings.

items.label: Traders
items.text: Market and wholesale traders: current accounts, seasonal balances.

items.label: Farmers and cooperatives
items.text: Harvest income, union and cooperative accounts.

items.label: Diaspora
items.text: Remittances, foreign currency and home-building savings.

items.label: MSMEs
items.text: Small firms needing payments, savings and later credit.

items.label: Institutions
items.text: Schools, NGOs, government offices, public enterprises.

items.label: Iddir, equb and religious bodies
items.text: Group savings and community funds.

example.title: Mapping the Hawassa Tabor branch
example.text: Meron Alemu, the new manager of Bank A's Hawassa Tabor branch (fictional), walked the catchment with two officers for a week. They counted a large public university campus, an industrial park with several thousand workers, the main market, four coffee and fruit cooperative unions in nearby woredas, many families receiving remittances and dozens of equb groups. The branch held Birr 1.2 billion of deposits, mostly from traders, and almost nothing from the industrial park or the cooperatives.

lessons.title: Community associations: iddir and equb
body: Iddir are community associations that support members at funerals and in hardship; equb are rotating savings groups where members contribute each period and take the pot in turn. Together they hold large sums, often in cash or in the personal account of a chairperson.

A bank can serve them with association accounts: the group's registration, by-laws and minutes naming signatories are collected, and the account is often run as an earmarked account. Members can later be offered personal accounts, and the regular equb cycle makes a natural link to save-for-credit products.

example.title: A 40-member equb in Shashemene
example.text: An equb of 40 traders in Shashemene collected Birr 5,000 from each member every week, Birr 200,000 in all, kept in cash by its chair, Ayelech Tadesse, until the weekly draw. After a theft scare, Bank A helped the group open an association account with two signatories named in its minutes. Weekly contributions are now deposited by mobile transfer and the winner is paid by transfer, and 15 members have opened personal savings accounts.

scenario.title: The equb chair's personal account
scenario.situation: The chair of an equb in Arba Minch asks to deposit the group's Birr 600,000 in his own savings account because it is quicker than opening a group account.
scenario.question: What should the officer do?
options: Accept, since the deposit is welcome either way
Open the account in the officer's name to save time
Refuse to serve equb groups because they are informal
Explain the risks to the members, and open an association account with the group's registration, by-laws and minutes naming signatories
scenario.explain: An association account protects members and gives the bank a clear mandate. A personal account leaves members exposed if the chair dies, leaves or misuses the funds.

lessons.title: Mobilization techniques
body: Banks use a range of techniques, each suited to some segments more than others. Campaigns in the branch work for walk-in customers. Agents reach villages and market areas far from a branch. Workplace and school drives bring many accounts at once. Digital onboarding lets customers open accounts by phone. Referral and cross-selling turn existing customers into a sales force.
The best plans combine several techniques, aim each at a named segment and set a target for accounts and birr for each.

items.label: Branch campaign
items.text: Posters, open days and service hours for walk-in customers.

items.label: Agent banking
items.text: Agents in villages and markets open accounts and take deposits.

items.label: Workplace and school drives
items.text: Payroll accounts for staff, savings accounts for pupils.

items.label: Digital onboarding
items.text: Account opening and wallet linking from a phone.

items.label: Referral and cross-selling
items.text: Existing customers bring new ones; every borrower also saves.

example.title: A payroll drive at the industrial park
example.text: Bank A agreed with a garment factory at the Hawassa industrial park to pay its 1,000 workers through Bank A accounts. Over two days, officers opened accounts on site using national ID, issued cards and showed workers how to save part of their wage automatically. The average balance was small, about Birr 6,000, but the deposits were stable and every account received money each month.

lessons.tip: Set the target per technique: 'payroll drive, 1,000 accounts, Birr 6 million' is a plan; 'increase deposits' is a wish.

lessons.title: Approaching and keeping depositors
body: Winning a depositor starts with understanding the need and ends long after the account is opened. Most deposit growth comes from customers who stay and add money, so retention matters as much as acquisition.

Large depositors deserve a named relationship officer, regular visits and quick service. When a competitor offers a higher rate, the answer is not always to match it: the officer should know the customer's whole relationship and escalate a rate request through the bank's approved pricing process.

items.label: See the need
items.text: Ask how the customer earns, saves and pays.

items.label: Explain clearly
items.text: Rates, charges and terms in plain words.

items.label: Recommend one fit
items.text: The product that matches the need, not the most expensive.

items.label: Verify
items.text: Complete KYC before the account is used.

items.label: Engage after
items.text: Follow up, reactivate, cross-sell.

scenario.title: A new bank offers one point more
scenario.situation: Abdi Mohammed, a coffee exporter in Dire Dawa, holds Birr 25 million in a Bank A time deposit maturing next week. A newly licensed bank has offered him 1 point more. Bank A's approved rate sheet allows the branch to offer up to 0.5 point extra on balances above Birr 10 million.
scenario.question: What should the relationship officer do first?
options: Warn him that new banks are unsafe
Let the money go, since rates are free
Promise to match the full 1 point to keep him
Meet him, review his whole relationship (current account, trade services, credit line), offer the approved 0.5 point and escalate a request for more through the pricing process
scenario.explain: The officer must stay within approved rates and escalate exceptions. Showing the value of the whole relationship often matters more than the last half point, and running down a competitor is unfair.

lessons.title: KYC at account opening and fair disclosure
body: Every account starts with knowing the customer. Staff identify the customer with a valid ID (the Fayda national digital ID is accepted alongside older IDs), take a photo, record the address and occupation, ask about the expected source and size of funds, screen names against lists and assign a risk rating. Group and business accounts also need their legal documents and a resolution naming signatories.

Fair treatment applies to deposits as much as to loans. Rates and charges must be disclosed clearly, advertising must not mislead, and complaints must be handled. A poster that says 'up to 15%' when that rate applies only to large three-year deposits is misleading unless the conditions are shown just as clearly.

items.label: Identify
items.text: Valid ID such as Fayda, photo, address.

items.label: Understand
items.text: Occupation, purpose, expected source and size of funds.

items.label: Screen
items.text: Check names against sanctions and internal lists.

items.label: Rate the risk
items.text: Low, medium or high; enhanced checks for high risk.

items.label: Disclose
items.text: Explain rates, charges and terms in writing.

regulation.source: NBE financial consumer protection directive FCP/01/2020 (reported) and NBE Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 41
regulation.text: The consumer protection directive, as reported, requires fair treatment, clear disclosure of rates and charges (including annual percentage rates), fair advertising, complaint handling and protection of customer data. The NBE Proclamation gives the NBE consumer protection duties over the institutions it supervises. Customer identification also follows Ethiopia's AML/CFT law and the NBE customer due diligence directive; check the current texts with your compliance unit.

scenario.title: The 'up to 15%' banner
scenario.situation: The Bahir Dar branch prints a banner reading 'Earn up to 15% on your savings!' The 15% applies only to fixed time deposits above Birr 5 million for three years; ordinary savings earn 8%.
scenario.question: What is the right action?
options: Remove or reprint it so the product, minimum amount and term are shown as clearly as the rate
Keep it: 'up to' makes it accurate
Add a small footnote in a corner
Replace it with the competitor's rate
scenario.explain: Fair advertising means the conditions are as visible as the headline rate. A hidden footnote still misleads ordinary savers.

lessons.title: Inactive and dormant accounts
body: Accounts with no customer activity for a long time become inactive and then dormant. Dormant accounts carry fraud risk, so banks restrict them: withdrawals need senior approval and the customer must update their information before the account is reactivated. Long-unclaimed balances follow the bank's and the law's procedure for unclaimed funds.

Dormant accounts are also a mobilization opportunity. Each one is a customer who already trusted the bank. A reactivation call, an updated KYC visit and a better-matched product can bring both the customer and new money back.

regulation.source: A commercial bank's operations procedures (typical Ethiopian bank manual)
regulation.text: A typical Ethiopian bank manual treats a checking account with no movement for 6 months as inactive and a savings account with no movement for 2 years as dormant. Withdrawals from dormant accounts need branch manager approval, and reactivation requires updated customer information. Check your own bank's current periods.

worked.title: Hawassa Tabor: dormant account reactivation drive

rows.label: Dormant savings accounts on the branch list
Customers reached by phone or visit
New money deposited by reactivated customers
Average new deposit per reactivated customer
Cost of calls, visits and SMS

worked.note: Reactivation cost less than 1% of the money it brought back, cheaper than most new-customer campaigns.

lessons.tip: Never reactivate a dormant account on a phone call alone: update the customer's KYC first.

lessons.title: Level 1 capstone: a 30-day plan for the Hawassa branch
body: The Level 1 capstone asks each group to build a 30-day deposit mobilization plan for a branch in a regional town, with target segments, products, channels and a birr target. Here is the plan Meron Alemu's team built for Bank A's Hawassa Tabor branch: Birr 60 million of new deposits and about 1,500 new or reactivated accounts in 30 days.

A good plan names each segment, the product offered, the channel, the number of accounts and the expected average balance, then adds up to the target. It also sets weekly checkpoints and a budget, so the manager can see early whether it is working.

items.label: Week 1
items.text: Agree payroll drive with the factory; visit cooperative unions; brief agents; print compliant materials.

items.label: Week 2
items.text: Industrial park and university drives; market day open desk; start dormant calls.

items.label: Week 3
items.text: Cooperative fixed time deposits; equb and iddir meetings; diaspora family evening.

items.label: Week 4
items.text: Referral push, follow-up of pending files, results against target, lessons learned.

worked.title: Hawassa Tabor 30-day plan (Birr)

rows.label: University and public staff: 250 accounts x 20,000
Cooperative unions: 4 fixed time deposits x 4,000,000

worked.note: Two segments, traders and cooperatives, bring more than half the birr with under 10% of the accounts, so they need the senior officers' time.

scenario.title: Where to put the best officers
scenario.situation: Meron has three experienced officers and four new ones. The cooperatives and traders bring Birr 34 million from 124 accounts; the payroll and university drives bring Birr 11 million from 1,250 accounts.
scenario.question: How should she allocate staff?
options: Skip the payroll drive because balances are small
Let each officer choose a segment
Send all experienced officers to the payroll drive because it has the most accounts
Put the experienced officers on cooperative and trader relationships, and the new officers on the payroll and university drives with a checklist and supervision
scenario.explain: Large relationships need negotiation and judgment; volume drives need careful, supervised processing. The payroll accounts are small but stable and should not be dropped.

takeaways: Map the catchment first: salaried staff, traders, farmers and cooperatives, diaspora, MSMEs, institutions, iddir and equb.
Iddir and equb should bank through association accounts with by-laws and minutes naming signatories, not a leader's personal account.
Combine branch campaigns, agents, workplace and school drives, digital onboarding and referrals, each with its own target.
Complete KYC before an account is used, disclose rates and charges clearly and never advertise a headline rate without its conditions.
Dormant accounts are a fraud risk and a cheap source of returning deposits; reactivate them only after a KYC update.
A 30-day plan names segment, product, channel, accounts and average balance, and adds up to the birr target.

quiz.q: What is an equb?
options: A type of fixed time deposit
A rotating savings group where members take the pot in turn
quiz.explain: Equb members contribute each period and receive the pooled amount in turn.

quiz.q: Which documents does a bank usually collect to open an iddir's account?
options: Registration, by-laws and minutes naming the signatories
quiz.explain: Association accounts need the group's registration, by-laws and minutes giving the mandate.

quiz.q: Which technique fits best for reaching 1,000 factory workers quickly?
quiz.explain: A workplace drive opens many payroll accounts at once with the employer's cooperation.

quiz.q: In a typical Ethiopian bank manual, when does a savings account become dormant?
quiz.explain: The typical manual sets 2 years of no movement for savings; checking accounts become inactive after 6 months.

quiz.q: A banner shows '15%' in large letters and the minimum amount in tiny print. What is wrong?
options: It is misleading: conditions must be as clear as the headline rate
The rate must be in foreign currency
quiz.explain: Fair advertising requires the conditions to be shown clearly with the rate.

quiz.q: In the Hawassa plan, what share of the Birr 60 million target do traders and cooperatives provide?
quiz.explain: Birr 18 million plus Birr 16 million is Birr 34 million, about 57% of Birr 60 million.

modules.title: Funding strategy, ALM and deposit pricing
modules.summary: Diagnose a bank's funding mix, concentration, loan-to-deposit ratio and cost of funds, then price deposits through funds transfer pricing and board-approved rates.
objectives: Analyse a bank's funding mix, core and volatile deposits and depositor concentration from five years of data
Calculate the loan-to-deposit ratio and judge the risk of a targeted reserve requirement
Compute the average and marginal cost of funds
Use funds transfer pricing to measure a branch's deposit contribution
Price a deposit product against the policy rate, competitor rates and inflation, within NBE/INT/13/2026

lessons.title: Reading five years of Bank A's deposit data
body: The Level 2 case gives learners five years of deposit data for Bank A, a mid-sized private bank. Total deposits grew from Birr 40 billion to Birr 66 billion, which looks healthy. The detail tells a different story.

Cheap savings and current accounts fell as a share of deposits while expensive time deposits rose. The 20 largest depositors grew from 18% to 31% of the total. The average cost of deposits rose from 6.1% to 9.2%, and the loan-to-deposit ratio reached 78.8%, above the private-bank average of 72.7% reported by the NBE in July 2026.

visual.caption: Bank A total deposits (fictional case data). Growth slowed from 17.5% in Year 2 to 10% in Year 5.

worked.title: Bank A: Year 1 against Year 5
worked.note: Bank A grew by buying expensive, concentrated time deposits to fund fast loan growth. That is the problem the three-year strategy must fix.

lessons.title: Core and volatile deposits
body: Core deposits are the stable part of the base: many small savings and payroll accounts whose total balance changes little even as individual customers come and go. Volatile deposits can leave quickly: large time deposits from a few institutions, rate-shopping customers and balances held for a single payment.

Core deposits can safely fund longer loans; volatile deposits must be matched with liquid assets. A bank that funds five-year loans with six-month institutional deposits is taking a liquidity risk that its ALCO must see and manage.

left.title: Core deposits
items: Many small savings and payroll accounts

right.title: Volatile deposits
items: Few large time deposits and institutions

example.title: A Birr 2 billion maturity
example.text: In Year 5 a public enterprise held a Birr 2 billion six-month time deposit at Bank A. At maturity it moved the money to another bank offering 0.75 point more. Bank A had to borrow Birr 1.2 billion overnight in the interbank market at about 14.6% for two weeks while it sold Treasury bills. The episode showed the ALCO how much of its base was volatile.

scenario.title: Funding a five-year loan
scenario.situation: Bank A's credit department wants to approve Birr 3 billion of five-year loans to manufacturers. The treasury notes that most new deposits this year were six-month institutional time deposits.
scenario.question: What should the ALCO ask for before agreeing the funding?
options: A higher rate on current accounts only
An analysis of core versus volatile deposits and a plan to raise stable or longer-term funding, or to limit the long loans
Approval to stop all savings accounts
scenario.explain: Long assets funded by short, volatile deposits create a funding gap. The ALCO needs to know how much of the base is truly stable and how the gap will be closed.

lessons.title: Concentration and the loan-to-deposit ratio
body: Concentration measures how much of the deposit base depends on a few customers. When the top 20 depositors hold 31% of Bank A's deposits, the loss of two or three of them could force the bank to borrow or sell assets at a bad time.

The loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) compares loans with deposits. A high LDR means the bank has lent most of its deposits and has little room left. In July 2026 the NBE introduced a targeted (additional) reserve requirement that it may impose on individual banks based on their LDR, so a high LDR can now carry a direct cost on top of the liquidity risk.

regulation.source: NBE Monetary Policy Committee meeting No. 7, press release of 13 July 2026
regulation.text: The NBE Board removed the credit growth cap, raised the National Bank Rate to 16% with the corridor of plus or minus 3 points unchanged, and introduced a targeted (additional) reserve requirement that the NBE may impose on individual banks based on their loan-to-deposit ratio. The release reported a private-bank loan-to-deposit ratio of 72.7%. The course inputs give no LDR threshold for the requirement; check the current NBE instruction for how it is applied.

worked.title: Bank A: concentration and LDR in Year 5
worked.note: Bank A needs about Birr 5.5 billion more deposits, or slower lending, just to return to the sector average.

scenario.title: The lending plan that outruns deposits
scenario.situation: The business plan proposes 25% loan growth next year, from Birr 52 billion to Birr 65 billion, while the deposit team expects 10% growth, from Birr 66 billion to Birr 72.6 billion.
scenario.question: What LDR would result, and what should the strategy team recommend?
options: About 89.5%; set a higher deposit target, slow loan growth or plan other funding before approving
scenario.explain: 65 divided by 72.6 is about 89.5%, well above the sector average and a likely trigger for a targeted reserve requirement. Lending and mobilization targets must be set together.

lessons.title: ALCO and the liquidity framework
body: The asset and liability committee (ALCO) brings together treasury, finance, risk, credit and business heads to manage the balance sheet. For resource mobilization it sets deposit targets and pricing ranges, watches concentration and the LDR, reviews liquidity gaps and approves the contingency funding plan.

Mobilization teams should feed the ALCO with facts: maturities of large deposits, rate requests from big customers, competitor rates and campaign results. The ALCO in turn gives the branches clear targets and pricing authority.

regulation.text: The guidelines expect banks to manage liquidity risk through an asset and liability committee, set liquidity limits, monitor maturity mismatches and run stress tests. The current liquid-asset ratio comes from the NBE liquidity directive; confirm the number with your treasury, as the latest text was not available for this course.

example.title: Bank A's contingency funding plan
example.text: After the Birr 2 billion maturity episode, Bank A's ALCO adopted a contingency funding plan. It lists early warning signs (a large depositor's notice, a fall in the liquid-asset ratio, a run of withdrawals at one branch), the first actions (sell Treasury bills, borrow in the interbank market, slow new loan disbursements) and who decides each step.

lessons.title: The cost of funds
body: The average cost of deposits is the weighted average of the rates paid on each product. It tells the bank what its existing base costs. The marginal cost is the rate the bank must pay to attract the next birr, which in a competitive market is usually higher.

The true cost of a deposit is also higher than its rate because part of it must be held in reserves, cash and liquid assets that earn little. Pricing decisions should use the marginal, reserve-adjusted cost, not the comfortable average.

visual.caption: Weights are each product's share of total deposits.

worked.title: Bank A: average and marginal cost of deposits, Year 5

rows.label: Year 1 on the same basis (55% x 7% + 25% x 9%)
Marginal cost: new one-year time deposits
Reserve-adjusted marginal cost if 10% earns nothing (assumption): 14.0 / 0.90

worked.note: The 10% non-earning share is a teaching assumption. At 15.6%, new time money costs almost as much as the 16% policy rate, leaving little margin on a 17.5% loan.

scenario.title: Average or marginal cost?
scenario.situation: The product manager proposes a new SME loan at 15.5%, arguing that Bank A's average cost of deposits is only 9.2%. The new loans will be funded by fresh one-year time deposits at 14%.
scenario.question: What is the main flaw in the argument?
options: Loans should be priced at the policy rate
The new loans will be funded at the marginal cost, about 15.6% after reserves, so a 15.5% loan loses money before operating costs and losses
The bank should use the interbank rate of 14.6% without adjustment
None; the average cost is the right benchmark
scenario.explain: Incremental business must be priced on the cost of the money that funds it. The average hides the cost of new funds.

lessons.title: Funds transfer pricing for branches
body: Funds transfer pricing (FTP) moves money inside the bank at internal rates. Treasury pays a branch an FTP rate for the deposits it raises and charges an FTP rate for the loans it makes. This shows which branches and products create value and stops branches from being judged only on their loan book.

A branch that raises cheap savings earns a good margin against the FTP rate; a branch that buys expensive time deposits earns little. FTP rates should follow market rates such as the interbank rate and Treasury bill yields, and stable deposits can earn a higher FTP credit than volatile ones.

worked.title: Hawassa Tabor branch: annual FTP contribution (illustrative rates)

rows.label: Loan yield minus FTP charge: 17.5% minus 13.0%
Total FTP margin before operating costs

worked.note: Two thirds of the branch's margin comes from deposits. Judged on loans alone, Hawassa Tabor would look like a weak branch.

example.title: Why the Mekelle branch stopped buying deposits
example.text: Bank A's Mekelle branch had the fastest deposit growth in the bank, but most of it came from time deposits at 14.5% and above. Once FTP was introduced at 12% for time money, the branch saw that each new birr lost 2.5 points. Its manager shifted the team to payroll and trader accounts, and its contribution rose within two quarters even though growth slowed.

lessons.title: Pricing a deposit product
body: A deposit rate is a business decision. The product team looks at the policy rate and interbank rate, the bank's FTP rate, competitor rates, inflation and customers' sensitivity, then proposes rates by product, term and balance band.

Under NBE/INT/13/2026 the rates must be approved in writing by the board on explicit written criteria and reported to the NBE. Branch staff must use only the approved rate sheet; exceptions go through the delegated pricing authority, never as private promises.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. NBE/INT/13/2026, Interest Rates (As Amended), in force 9 January 2026
regulation.text: Deposit and lending rates are set freely by each bank, approved in writing by its board on explicit written criteria. A bank reports its rates to the NBE within 5 working days of a change and its monthly weighted average rates within 7 working days. Existing contracts keep their agreed terms.

scenario.title: Answering a 15% competitor
scenario.situation: A new bank advertises 15% on one-year time deposits. Bank A pays 13.5%. The policy rate is 16%, the 7-day interbank rate 14.6%, Bank A's FTP credit for one-year time money 13.0% and its average loan yield 17.5%.
scenario.question: What is the soundest response for Bank A's ALCO?
options: Cut the time deposit rate to 12% to protect the margin
Match 15% for all customers at once
Ask the NBE to cap competitors' rates
Keep 13.5% for the general rate, offer a higher approved band only to large, stable relationships where the whole relationship is profitable, and push cheaper savings and payroll accounts
scenario.explain: A 15% rate for everyone would cost more than the FTP credit and squeeze the 17.5% loan margin. Targeted pricing and a better mix protect both the base and the margin. The NBE no longer caps or floors deposit rates.

takeaways: Headline deposit growth can hide a worse mix, higher concentration and a rising cost of funds.
Core deposits can fund longer loans; volatile deposits need matching liquid assets.
The LDR now carries a direct risk: the NBE may impose a targeted reserve requirement on banks with a high ratio.
Price new business on the marginal, reserve-adjusted cost of funds, not the average.
Funds transfer pricing shows the value branches create by raising cheap, stable deposits.
Deposit rates need written board approval and NBE reporting within 5 working days of a change; staff use only approved rates.

quiz.q: Bank A has loans of Birr 52 billion and deposits of Birr 66 billion. What is its LDR?
quiz.explain: 52 divided by 66 is about 78.8%.

quiz.q: Which deposits are usually the most volatile?
options: Large time deposits from a few institutions
quiz.explain: Large institutional time deposits are rate sensitive and can leave at maturity.

quiz.q: Why should new loans be priced on marginal rather than average cost?
options: New loans are funded by new money at today's market cost
quiz.explain: Incremental assets are funded at the price of the next birr raised.

quiz.q: Within how many working days must a bank report a change in its rates to the NBE?
quiz.explain: NBE/INT/13/2026 sets 5 working days for rate changes and 7 for monthly weighted averages.

quiz.q: A branch's deposits cost 8.4% and the FTP credit is 12.0%. What is the deposit margin on Birr 500 million?
quiz.explain: (12.0% minus 8.4%) x 500 million is Birr 18 million.

quiz.q: What new tool linked to the LDR did the NBE introduce in July 2026?
quiz.explain: MPC No. 7 introduced a targeted reserve requirement the NBE may impose based on a bank's LDR.

modules.title: Segment strategies and digital mobilization
modules.summary: Design strategies for diaspora, institutional, MSME and unbanked rural customers, and use agents, mobile money links, Fayda eKYC and customer data to grow cheap, stable deposits.
objectives: Design deposit strategies for diaspora, institutional and government, MSME and rural customers
Weigh the cost, size and stability of institutional deposits against their concentration risk
Evaluate agent banking and mobile money partnerships as mobilization channels
Use Fayda eKYC and customer data to design digital savings products and targeted campaigns

lessons.title: Diaspora: remittance-linked accounts, bonds and shares
body: The diaspora is one of the few segments that brings both birr deposits and foreign currency. Since the July 2024 move to a market-based exchange rate, sending money through banks is far more attractive than before, and banks compete on speed, digital access and products linked to remittances.

A diaspora strategy usually combines remittance-linked accounts for families at home, foreign currency and birr accounts for the senders, savings products for home building and business, and, where the bank raises capital, offers of bank shares or bonds to diaspora investors through the proper public offer process.

items.label: Remittance-linked account
items.text: Money from abroad lands in a family member's account, not cash.

items.label: Foreign currency account
items.text: Savings kept in foreign currency under FXD/01/2024.

items.label: Home-building savings
items.text: A goal account that leads to a mortgage.

items.label: Shares and bonds
items.text: Capital raising offered to diaspora investors through a proper offer.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. FXD/01/2024, as amended by FXD/04/2026
regulation.text: FXD/01/2024 provides for foreign currency accounts for non-resident Ethiopians and foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin under freely negotiated exchange rates. FXD/04/2026 removed the minimum foreign currency account deposit and lets FDI companies open foreign currency accounts with only an application, investment licence and TIN.

example.title: Bank A's diaspora desk
example.text: Bank A set up a diaspora desk with two officers who answer calls in the evening Ethiopian time, when customers in North America are awake. They open accounts online, link each sender to a family account in Ethiopia and offer a home-building savings plan. In its first year, the desk opened 2,400 accounts and raised Birr 1.8 billion of birr and foreign currency deposits, all in small and medium balances.

lessons.title: Institutional and government deposits
body: Schools, universities, NGOs, regional bureaus and public enterprises hold large balances. Winning them can add hundreds of millions of birr in one decision, but these deposits are often concentrated, rate sensitive and won through tenders. They may also leave at the end of a budget year or a project.

The best institutional relationships are built on service, not only rate: cash management, payroll, collection accounts, quick reporting and online banking. A bank should know the timing of each institution's cash flows and match them with liquid assets.

scenario.title: A regional bureau's tender
scenario.situation: A regional bureau offers Birr 1.5 billion for six months to the bank that bids the highest rate. Bank A's ALCO is worried about its 78.8% LDR and 31% top-20 concentration. A bid of 15% would win; Bank A's FTP credit for six-month money is 12.5%.
scenario.question: What should the ALCO decide?
options: Bid 15% because the deposit lowers the LDR

Bid only if the money can be placed at a positive margin (for example in liquid assets until loans are ready) and the maturity is matched, accepting that it adds concentration; otherwise decline and bid for the bureau's payroll and collection accounts
Bid 18% to be sure of winning
scenario.explain: The deposit would lower the LDR but cost 2.5 points more than the FTP credit and add a large six-month maturity. Service-based business from the same client is cheaper and more stable.

example.title: A university's collection account
example.text: Instead of bidding for a public university's term deposit, Bank A offered to collect its student fees through mobile transfers and its branches, and to pay its 2,000 staff. The university's average balance at Bank A rose to Birr 180 million, almost all in current and savings accounts at low cost, and most staff opened personal accounts.

lessons.title: MSMEs and unbanked rural customers through agents
body: Many Ethiopians still have no bank account, especially in rural areas and among women. The national financial inclusion strategies (NFIS-II for 2021 to 2025 and the NFIS-III refresh) aim to close this gap through digital channels and agents. For a bank, every new account in an unbanked area is a long-term depositor and future borrower.

Agents are shops, cooperatives or kiosks that open accounts and take deposits and withdrawals for the bank. They cost far less than a branch. They need training, liquidity support, close monitoring and clear commission rules, under the NBE's agent banking and payment rules.

worked.title: Bank A: 25 agents in Sidama zone villages, one month (illustrative)

rows.label: New accounts per agent per month
Agent commissions and support: 25 x Birr 4,000
Acquisition cost as a share of first-month deposits

worked.note: The first month looks expensive, but balances grow as farmers deposit harvest income. Compare it with the cost of opening one branch.

scenario.title: Choosing the next channel
scenario.situation: Bank A plans to reach five rural kebeles near Hawassa with about 25,000 unbanked adults. Option A is a new branch costing Birr 12 million to fit out plus Birr 6 million a year. Option B is 30 agents with tablets, costing Birr 1.5 million to set up and Birr 1.4 million a year.
scenario.question: Which approach makes most sense first?
options: Start with agents, monitor accounts, balances and agent liquidity, and add a branch only if volumes justify it
Do nothing until NFIS-III targets are published
Ask the cooperatives to collect cash for the bank informally
Build the branch, since customers trust branches more
scenario.explain: Agents reach dispersed customers at a fraction of the cost and can be scaled. Informal cash collection outside the agent rules is not permitted.

lessons.title: Competing and partnering with mobile money
body: Telecom-led mobile money, such as telebirr and M-PESA, has signed up millions of Ethiopians and holds balances that once sat in bank accounts. Banks compete with it for everyday transactions, but they can also partner with it: wallet-to-account transfers let customers move money into savings, and bank products can be offered inside wallet menus.

The bank's strength is what a wallet does not offer: interest or profit-sharing savings, time deposits, larger balances, credit and a relationship. The strategy is to make it easy to move money from wallet to account and to give customers a reason to keep it there.

right.title: Bank account
items: Savings and time deposits that earn
Linked to the wallet for easy transfers

regulation.source: National Payment System Proclamation No. 718/2011 as amended by No. 1282/2023 (reported), and NBE payment instrument issuer directives
regulation.text: The payment system law, as reported, governs payment instrument issuers, e-money and payment system operators. Wallet providers and banks link accounts and wallets within this framework and the NBE's directives on payment instrument issuers and agents; check the current directive numbers with your digital banking unit.

example.title: From wallet to savings
example.text: Bank A launched a 'sweep to save' feature: customers who link their wallet to a Bank A account can set an amount, such as Birr 200 each week, to move automatically into savings. Selam Tesfaye, a hairdresser in Adama, saved Birr 10,400 in a year without visiting a branch, and later used her savings record to get a small equipment loan.

lessons.title: Fayda eKYC and digital onboarding
body: The Fayda national digital ID lets banks verify a customer's identity electronically. Combined with a phone, it allows accounts to be opened in minutes from anywhere, which cuts the cost of acquisition and reaches customers who never visit a branch.

Digital onboarding still needs good controls: confirm the ID against the national system, capture a live photo, apply transaction limits to low-risk accounts opened remotely, screen names and move the customer to full KYC if activity grows.

items.label: Download or dial
items.text: Customer starts on the app or a USSD menu.

items.label: Verify Fayda ID
items.text: ID number checked electronically, live photo taken.

items.label: Screen and rate
items.text: Names screened, a risk tier and limits assigned.

items.label: Open and fund
items.text: Account opened; first deposit from a wallet or agent.

items.label: Upgrade
items.text: Full KYC when balances or activity exceed the tier.

scenario.title: A surge of remote accounts
scenario.situation: Bank A's digital channel opened 8,000 remote accounts in a month. Monitoring shows 40 accounts receiving many small transfers from different senders and sending the total abroad through one wallet.
scenario.question: What should the digital team do?
options: Restrict the 40 accounts, review them with compliance and report suspicious activity as required, then tighten monitoring rules
Raise the limits to keep the customers happy
Ignore it, since each transfer is small
scenario.explain: Digital growth needs monitoring that can spot unusual patterns. Acting on the flagged accounts and fixing the rules protects the channel without stopping it.

lessons.title: Data-driven campaigns and digital savings products
body: Banks already hold rich data: salary inflows, wallet transfers, seasonal patterns and product holdings. Analysing it shows who could save more, who is likely to leave and which product fits. A targeted message to the right 20,000 customers beats a poster aimed at everyone.

Digital savings products work best when they are simple and automatic: goal accounts for school fees or a home, round-up savings on card payments, weekly sweeps from a wallet, and small time deposits opened in the app.

worked.title: Bank A: targeted goal-savings campaign

rows.label: Customers with regular salary inflows but no savings balance
Response rate to a personal SMS and app offer
Campaign cost (SMS, app work, staff time)
Cost as a share of new deposits

worked.note: The cost is lower than the agent channel in its first month and the balances come from existing customers whose identity is already known.

scenario.title: Which customers to target first?
scenario.situation: The data team can run only one campaign this quarter. List A: 20,000 salaried customers with no savings. List B: 3,000 customers whose balances fell more than 50% in three months. List C: 50,000 customers who have not used the app in a year.
scenario.question: Which list should come first to protect and grow deposits?
options: List B, because these customers may be leaving and each retained one keeps an existing balance; then List A
All three with the same message
List C, because it is the largest
scenario.explain: A falling balance is an early sign of attrition. Retention calls to List B protect money already in the bank; List A is the next best growth opportunity.

takeaways: Diaspora strategy links remittances, foreign currency accounts, goal savings and, where relevant, capital offers.
Institutional deposits are large but concentrated and rate sensitive; win them with service, not only rate.
Agents reach unbanked rural customers at a fraction of a branch's cost, within the NBE's agent and payment rules.
Partner with mobile money: make wallet-to-account transfers easy and give customers a reason to save in the bank.
Fayda eKYC enables fast remote onboarding, but tiered limits and monitoring must come with it.
Use customer data to target retention first and growth second, with simple, automatic digital savings products.

quiz.q: What makes the diaspora segment special for a bank's funding?
options: It brings both birr deposits and foreign currency
quiz.explain: Remittances and diaspora accounts add birr and foreign currency at the same time.

quiz.q: Which change did FXD/04/2026 make to foreign currency accounts?
options: Raised the minimum deposit to USD 1,000
Removed the minimum foreign currency account deposit
quiz.explain: FXD/04/2026 removed the minimum foreign currency account deposit.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a large institutional time deposit?
options: Concentration and the chance it leaves at maturity
It must be in foreign currency
quiz.explain: Large institutional balances are concentrated and rate sensitive.

quiz.q: Twenty-five agents each open 40 accounts with an average balance of Birr 3,000. What are the new deposits?
quiz.explain: 25 x 40 x 3,000 is Birr 3.0 million.

quiz.q: What should accompany remote account opening with Fayda eKYC?
options: Tiered limits, screening and monitoring, with full KYC when activity grows
A branch visit for every account
quiz.explain: Remote onboarding is safe when limits and monitoring match the risk.

quiz.q: A bank's main advantage over a mobile wallet is usually:
options: Earning savings and time deposits, larger balances and credit
quiz.explain: Wallets are strong in payments; banks offer earning deposits and credit.

modules.title: Non-deposit resources, performance and the three-year strategy
modules.summary: Compare interbank, NBE facilities, bonds, subordinated debt, equity and development finance lines, manage mobilization with scorecards and campaign returns, and present Bank A's three-year strategy.
objectives: Compare the cost, tenor and conditions of interbank borrowing, NBE standing facilities, bonds, subordinated debt, equity and DFI lines
Explain how capital rules and new entrants under SBB/94/2025 shape a bank's funding and capital plans
Build a branch scorecard and calculate the return on a mobilization campaign
Present a three-year resource mobilization strategy with targets consistent with lending plans and the LDR

lessons.title: The interbank market and NBE standing facilities
body: When deposits fall short, a bank can borrow short-term money from other banks in the interbank market, at rates negotiated between them; the 7-day interbank rate was 14.6% in mid-2026. As a last line, it can use the NBE's standing lending facility, priced above the policy rate.

With a corridor of plus or minus 3 points around the 16% National Bank Rate, the standing lending facility sits near 19% and the standing deposit facility near 13%. Interbank and NBE money is useful for days or weeks, not for funding loans for years. A bank that relies on it every month has a structural funding gap.

visual.caption: Market rates from the MPC No. 7 release (July 2026); Bank A's rates are fictional case data.

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Arts. 29 and 30
regulation.text: Article 29 gives the NBE its monetary instruments, including credit operations, open market operations, standing deposit, overnight lending and intraday facilities, and reserve requirements. Article 30 makes the NBE lender of last resort at a rate above the policy rate. Rates on NBE lending and standing facilities are set by the NBE (NBE/INT/13/2026).

scenario.title: Borrowing to fund loans
scenario.situation: Bank A's treasury has borrowed Birr 1.5 billion in the 7-day interbank market at about 14.6% and rolled it every week for three months to fund new term loans.
scenario.question: What should the ALCO conclude?
options: It is fine because the rate is below the policy rate
Report a profit on the borrowing
Move the borrowing to the standing lending facility to save cost
It is a structural funding gap: short money is funding long loans, and the bank needs stable deposits or term funding, or slower lending
scenario.explain: Rolling weekly borrowing to fund term loans exposes the bank to rate rises and market closure. The standing lending facility, near 19%, would cost more, not less.

lessons.title: Subordinated debt and corporate bonds
body: Since the Ethiopian Securities Exchange launched in January 2025, banks can consider raising longer-term money through bonds sold to investors. Senior bonds give term funding; subordinated debt ranks behind depositors and may support capital if it meets the capital directive's conditions.

Bonds need a prospectus, approval from the Ethiopian Capital Market Authority and investors willing to buy at a rate that reflects inflation and the policy rate. They suit a bank that needs money for three to seven years, such as funding long-term project and mortgage loans.

regulation.source: ECMA Directive on public offer and trading of securities (reported as No. 1030/2024), under Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021
regulation.text: As reported, a public offer of securities needs a prospectus and registration with the ECMA, and a private placement is limited to 100 investors. A bank considering subordinated debt must also check whether it meets the conditions of the NBE capital adequacy directive SBB/95/2025 (total capital at least 11% of risk-weighted assets).

example.title: A five-year bond for mortgages
example.text: Bank A's board considered a Birr 2 billion five-year bond to fund mortgage loans for diaspora and salaried customers. Advisers suggested a coupon of about 15% given the 16% policy rate and inflation. The ALCO compared it with one-year time deposits at 13.5%: the bond cost more, but it fixed the funding for five years and matched the mortgages, which time deposits could not.

lessons.title: Equity, rights issues and new entrants
body: Equity is the most permanent resource. It absorbs losses, supports lending under the capital adequacy directive and is needed to meet the minimum paid-up capital. Many Ethiopian banks have used rights issues to work toward the Birr 5 billion minimum paid-up capital due by June 2026, and pressure to consolidate remains for banks that struggle to reach it.

Competition for funds is also changing. SBB/94/2025 lets foreign banks enter as subsidiaries or branches with Birr 5 billion of capital, and lets foreign investors buy into new domestic banks, which will bring new competitors for large depositors and diaspora customers.

regulation.source: NBE Directives SBB/78/2021 (reported) and SBB/94/2025 (in force 25 June 2025)
regulation.text: SBB/78/2021, as reported, sets a minimum paid-up capital of Birr 5 billion for existing banks by 30 June 2026. SBB/94/2025 requires Birr 5 billion for a new bank, a foreign bank subsidiary or a foreign bank branch and USD 100,000 for a representative office, and caps a foreign strategic investor at 40% and all foreign holders at 49% of a new domestic bank. Capital adequacy under SBB/95/2025 requires CET1 of 7%, Tier 1 of 9% and total capital of 11% of risk-weighted assets.

worked.title: Bank A: a one-for-five rights issue

rows.label: Offer: 1 new share for every 5 held, at par
New capital raised if fully taken up: 5.2 / 5
Extra lending supported at an 11% total capital ratio (100% risk weight, illustrative): 1.04 / 0.11

worked.note: Equity does not replace deposits: Bank A still needs the deposits to fund the extra Birr 9.5 billion of loans the new capital can support.

scenario.title: Capital or deposits?
scenario.situation: A board member says Bank A's rights issue of Birr 1.04 billion 'solves the funding problem'.
scenario.question: How should the strategy head respond?
options: Suggest paying the new capital out as dividends
Explain that the new capital allows more lending under the capital rules, but the loans still have to be funded mostly by deposits, so the mobilization targets stay
scenario.explain: Capital and funding are different constraints. Capital supports risk; deposits and other liabilities fund the balance sheet.

lessons.title: Development finance lines
body: Development finance institutions such as the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the European Investment Bank provide credit lines to Ethiopian banks for on-lending to MSMEs, agriculture, women entrepreneurs or green projects, often through government programs.

These lines bring long tenors and technical support, but they come with eligibility rules, reporting, environmental and social standards and, if in foreign currency, exchange rate risk that must be managed. They complement deposits for specific portfolios; they do not replace them.

left.title: Deposits
items: Cost set by the market and the bank
Free to lend to any sound borrower

right.title: DFI credit lines
items: Long tenor, often with grace periods
Foreign currency lines carry exchange rate risk

example.title: An MSME line for women entrepreneurs
example.text: Bank A joined a DFI-funded program for women-led MSMEs, receiving a Birr 600 million line for on-lending over seven years. The line came with training for loan officers and a reporting template. Bank A used it alongside a women's savings account, so borrowers also became depositors: two years later, borrowers under the line held Birr 140 million in savings.

lessons.title: Branch scorecards, KPIs and campaign return
body: What gets measured gets managed. A mobilization scorecard tracks more than total deposits: the mix of low-cost deposits, the number of active accounts, retention, concentration, cost of deposits and the FTP contribution. It rewards branches for cheap, stable growth, not for buying expensive money.
Each campaign should be judged after it ends: how much was raised, how much stayed after 90 days, what margin it earns and what it cost.

items.label: Deposit growth
items.text: Net growth against target, by product.

items.label: Low-cost share
items.text: Savings and current accounts as a share of deposits.

items.label: Active accounts
items.text: Accounts with activity in the last 90 days.

items.label: Retention
items.text: Share of campaign money still there after 90 days.

items.label: Concentration
items.text: Top 20 depositors' share of branch deposits.

items.label: FTP contribution
items.text: Margin earned on deposits against the FTP rate.

worked.title: Hawassa Tabor 30-day campaign: return after 90 days

rows.label: New deposits raised in 30 days (target Birr 60 million)
Still in the bank after 90 days: 85%
Annual margin on retained deposits: 44.2 x 3.6%

worked.note: The branch missed the birr target by 13%, but the campaign paid back its cost more than three times in its first year because most of the money stayed.

scenario.title: Two branches, two stories
scenario.situation: Branch X grew deposits 30% in a year, mostly with time deposits at 14.5%. Branch Y grew 12%, mostly savings and payroll accounts, and raised its low-cost share from 50% to 58%. The FTP credit for time money is 12%.
scenario.question: Which branch should the scorecard rank higher?
options: Neither, because both missed a 40% target
Branch X, because growth is all that matters
Branch Y, because its growth is cheaper and more stable and earns a positive FTP margin, while Branch X loses margin on most new money
scenario.explain: At 14.5% against a 12% FTP credit, Branch X loses 2.5 points on its new money. A balanced scorecard rewards Branch Y's quality of growth.

lessons.title: Level 2 capstone: Bank A's three-year strategy
body: The Level 2 capstone asks learners to diagnose Bank A's five years of data and present a three-year resource mobilization strategy to a mock management committee. A strong strategy starts from the lending plan, sets deposit targets that keep the LDR safely below the level that could attract a targeted reserve requirement, and fixes the mix and concentration problems.

It combines the tools of this course: segment strategies (payroll, traders, diaspora, rural agents), digital mobilization, pricing through FTP and approved rate bands, selected non-deposit funding for long assets, a capital plan and a scorecard to track it all.

items.label: Year 1
items.text: Fix pricing and FTP; launch payroll, trader and diaspora programs; cap new large time deposits; reach LDR below 77%.

items.label: Year 2
items.text: Scale agents and wallet links in rural areas; Fayda onboarding; consider a five-year bond for mortgages; top 20 below 26%.

items.label: Year 3
items.text: Low-cost share above 60%; LDR near 75%; cost of deposits below 8.8%; deposits about Birr 90 billion.

worked.title: Bank A three-year targets (from Year 5 to Year 8)

rows.label: Deposits: 66.0 growing about 11% a year (66 x 1.11 x 1.11 x 1.11)

worked.note: Loan growth of 9% a year is slower than the past but is fully funded by deposits, keeping the LDR near 75%.

scenario.title: The management committee's challenge
scenario.situation: During the mock presentation, the CEO asks why the strategy targets loan growth of only 9% a year when the credit cap has been removed and demand is strong.
scenario.question: What is the best answer?
options: Say the NBE still limits credit growth

Show that faster lending without matching deposits would push the LDR toward 90%, risking a targeted reserve requirement and liquidity stress, and offer a higher loan path only if deposit or term funding targets are beaten
Say the bank should stop lending until deposits recover
Promise 25% loan growth to please the committee
scenario.explain: The credit cap is gone, but funding and the LDR now set the limit. Linking any faster lending to proven funding is the disciplined answer.

takeaways: Interbank and NBE standing facilities are for short gaps; the standing lending facility sits near 19% with a 16% policy rate.
Bonds and subordinated debt can give term funding for long assets, through the ECMA public offer process.
Equity supports lending under SBB/95/2025 and meets the Birr 5 billion minimum, but loans still need to be funded.
DFI lines bring long tenor for specific programs, with eligibility, reporting and exchange rate conditions.
Scorecards should reward cheap, stable growth: low-cost share, active accounts, retention, concentration and FTP margin.
A three-year strategy starts from the lending plan and sets deposit, mix, concentration and cost targets that keep the LDR safe.

quiz.q: With a 16% policy rate and a corridor of plus or minus 3 points, where does the standing lending facility sit?
quiz.explain: 16 plus 3 is 19%.

quiz.q: What does rolling 7-day interbank borrowing every week to fund term loans indicate?
quiz.explain: Short borrowing funding long loans signals a structural gap.

quiz.q: What minimum paid-up capital did existing banks have to reach by 30 June 2026, as reported?
quiz.explain: SBB/78/2021, as reported, set Birr 5 billion.

quiz.q: A campaign keeps Birr 44.2 million earning a 3.6% margin and cost Birr 0.45 million. What is its first-year return?
quiz.explain: Margin of Birr 1.59 million minus cost of 0.45 million, divided by 0.45, is about 253%.

quiz.q: What is a typical condition of a DFI credit line?
options: It must be repaid in 30 days
Eligibility rules and environmental and social standards
quiz.explain: DFI lines come with eligibility, reporting and E&S conditions.

quiz.q: Under SBB/94/2025, what is the most a single foreign strategic investor may hold in a new domestic bank?
quiz.explain: The cap is 40% per strategic investor and 49% for all foreign holders together.

exam.q: Bank A's deposits are Birr 66 billion of a Birr 82 billion balance sheet. About what share of its funding do deposits provide?
exam.explain: 66 divided by 82 is about 80%.

exam.q: A bank lends 75% of a Birr 1,000,000 deposit at 17.5% and pays 8% on the deposit. What is its net interest income on that deposit?
exam.explain: 131,250 earned minus 80,000 paid is Birr 51,250.

exam.q: A one-year time deposit pays 13.5% while inflation is 13.4%. What is the real return?
exam.explain: (1.135 / 1.134) minus 1 is about plus 0.1%.

exam.q: A customer insists the bank must pay the NBE minimum savings rate of 7%. What is correct?
options: There is no minimum since NBE/INT/13/2026; each bank's board sets its rates
The minimum applies only to state banks
The minimum still applies to savings only
exam.explain: NBE/INT/13/2026 removed the minimum deposit rate.

exam.q: A mudarabah depositor's return depends on:
options: The actual profit of the investment, shared by an agreed ratio
exam.explain: Mudarabah is profit sharing by a ratio agreed in advance.

exam.q: A diaspora foreign currency account receives a credit from a local birr supplier. What is the right response?
options: Correct it as an error under the bank's procedure and record the exception
exam.explain: Diaspora FCY accounts are funded from abroad in foreign currency.

exam.q: Which approach gives an equb the best protection?
options: An association account with by-laws and minutes naming signatories
An account in a branch officer's name
Deposits in the chair's personal account
exam.explain: An association account gives a clear mandate and protects members.

exam.q: A savings rate is advertised at 15% while 15% applies only to three-year deposits above Birr 5 million. The minimum fix is to:
options: Show the product, minimum and term as clearly as the rate
exam.explain: Fair advertising needs conditions as visible as the headline rate.

exam.q: A dormant account holder phones to ask for an urgent transfer. What should the branch do?
options: Require a KYC update and senior approval under the bank's procedure before reactivating
exam.explain: Dormant accounts are reactivated only after updated customer information and approval.

exam.q: In a 30-day plan, 120 traders with an average Birr 150,000 and 4 cooperatives at Birr 4,000,000 each bring how much?
exam.explain: 18 million plus 16 million is Birr 34 million.

exam.q: Loans are expected to reach Birr 65 billion and deposits Birr 72.6 billion. What is the LDR and the main risk?
options: About 89.5%; liquidity stress and a possible targeted reserve requirement
exam.explain: 65 / 72.6 is about 89.5%, well above the 72.7% private-bank average.

exam.q: Savings are 42% of deposits at 8%, current 15% at 0% and time 43% at 13.5%. What is the average cost?
exam.explain: 3.36 plus 0 plus 5.81 is about 9.2%.

exam.q: New time deposits cost 14% and 10% of each deposit earns nothing. What is the reserve-adjusted cost?
exam.explain: 14 divided by 0.90 is about 15.6%.

exam.q: A branch raises Birr 800 million at a cost of 9.0% with an FTP credit of 12.0%. What is its deposit margin?
exam.explain: (12.0% minus 9.0%) x 800 million is Birr 24 million.

exam.q: Which statement about deposit rates under NBE/INT/13/2026 is correct?
options: Rates must equal the National Bank Rate
The NBE sets a ceiling on time deposit rates
Branch managers may set any rate
Rates need written board approval on explicit criteria and reporting to the NBE
exam.explain: The directive requires board approval in writing and NBE reporting.

exam.q: A regional bureau offers Birr 1.5 billion for six months at 15%; the FTP credit is 12.5%. What is the main concern?
options: Negative margin and a large concentrated maturity
It cannot be accepted by law
exam.explain: It costs 2.5 points over FTP and adds a six-month concentration.

exam.q: Which channel usually reaches dispersed unbanked rural customers at the lowest cost?
options: A new branch in every kebele
exam.explain: Agents with digital onboarding scale at a fraction of a branch's cost.

exam.q: Bank A raises Birr 1.04 billion of new capital. At an 11% total capital ratio and 100% risk weights, about how much extra lending can it support?
exam.explain: 1.04 divided by 0.11 is about Birr 9.5 billion, which still needs funding.

exam.q: Why is rolling weekly interbank borrowing a poor way to fund five-year loans?
options: Interbank rates are fixed for five years
It exposes the bank to rate rises and market closure on long assets
exam.explain: Short funding of long assets creates rollover and rate risk.

exam.q: A strategy targets deposits of Birr 90.3 billion and loans of Birr 67.5 billion in three years. What LDR results?
exam.explain: 67.5 divided by 90.3 is about 74.8%.
